frase_gancho.texto: A painted paradise where the water never runs out.

puente_narrativo.texto: Look at a detail of the mural: men striking a ball with curved sticks. From the painted game we move on to the game in stone, with a marker that can be taken apart, used by the residents of another neighborhood of the city.

guion_corto.texto: What you see is a reproduction of a mural from Portico 2 of Tepantitla, a residential compound in Teotihuacán. It was painted in fresco by the restorer Agustín Villagra. Above, a figure with open arms lets drops of water, seeds and jewels fall, beneath a sacred tree where birds and butterflies flutter. Below, a green hill pours rivers into a pond, and people swim, sing, gather fruit and play ball. Alfonso Caso interpreted it as the Tlalocan, the paradise of the rain god, where those who died by water or by lightning went. Look at the mouths of the figures: flowers come out of them. They are words and songs. It is the ideal world, seen from Teotihuacán.

guion_largo.texto:
Teotihuacán was not only temples and pyramids. It was also a city of neighborhoods: large residential compounds with courtyards and porticoes, where many people lived. And in those homes there were paintings on the walls. Tepantitla was one of those compounds, east of the Pyramid of the Sun, and the mural was on a wall of its Portico 2. In other words: this scene was not painted in a distant temple, but in a place where people lived.

What you have in front of you is a reproduction, painted by Agustín Villagra, a restorer who devoted years to copying ancient murals with the same fresco technique. Why copy them? Because the originals cannot be moved without being destroyed, and because over time their colors fade. The copy lets you see the whole scene, with the intensity it may once have had. In this very hall there are other reproductions by Villagra: it is part of the work the museum did in 1964 so that visitors could see what the ruin no longer shows.

Look at the upper level. There is a large figure with open arms, from which drops of water, seeds and jewels fall. Alfonso Caso, who studied the mural in the twentieth century, saw her as Tláloc; today many specialists call her the Great Goddess of Teotihuacán. Above her rises a tree with twisted, flowering branches, with birds and butterflies. On either side there are small figures that seem to sing or pray. It is an image of generosity: everything good comes from above and descends to the earth.

Now lower your gaze. A green hill, from which springs flow, pours its water toward a pond. Tiny figures swim, others sing, others gather fruit, others play. There are seeds, plants, butterflies. From the mouths of the figures come curled lines with flowers, which represent speech and song: for the peoples of Mesoamerica, speaking well and singing was a way of blossoming, and that is why poetry was called “flower and song.” You will see that idea very much alive among the Mexica, in the Mexica Hall.

Alfonso Caso called this scene the Tlalocan because of an idea that we know the Mexica held, centuries later: the Tlalocan was the paradise of the rain god, where those who died by drowning, by lightning, or by certain illnesses linked to water went. There was plenty of food there, there were festivities, and drought never came. If you remember the fish vessel from the previous hall, here water again fills with life, with the same respect.

Not everyone accepts that reading. The mural carries no inscription, and the Mexica lived a thousand years later; we do not know whether the people of Teotihuacán thought the same way. The specialist Esther Pasztory, for example, proposed that the scene is not an afterlife, but a celebration of water and the mountain that feeds everyone. Whether it is paradise or celebration, the message does not change: water brings abundance, and a city that depends on water paints it in its homes.

Notice also the ball game played with sticks. It appears painted in a corner of the scene, and it is one of the few images we have of how the game was played in Teotihuacán, a city where the long courts that did exist in other parts of Mesoamerica have not been found. The mural and the piece that follows explain each other: one shows the action; the other, an object from the game.

Close your eyes for a moment and think about the contrast: what dominates is not war or power, but celebration: people who swim, who sing, who eat. Perhaps that is why this mural moves us so much: it shows us one of the most powerful cities of the ancient world imagining, for its dead and for its living, a place of joy.

texto: Find the green hill where the water springs forth
Find the figures that sing: what comes out of their mouths?
Look at the players’ curved sticks and find the ball

texto.Material: Fresco on stucco and lime mortar, with mineral pigments of red hematite, green malachite, and yellow limonite
texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (Tepantitla residential compound, east of the Pyramid of the Sun)
texto.Discovery: Discovered in 1942 by the archaeologist Alfonso Caso in the Tepantitla residential compound

texto.pregunta: Myth: This mural is an original painting from fifteen hundred years ago, moved to the museum.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a fresco reproduction painted by Agustín Villagra; the original was painted in a residential compound in Teotihuacán.
